questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Other

questions.question: Please explain: *
questions.answer: Travels combined with living far away

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer:
1) English speaking country
2) Far away
3) Cool city

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: Very easy, everything is sent via e-mails.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: Mails and I seeked out further assistance at the student help service at campus (Stop1). They're very helpful with everything both via e-mail and in person.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer:
It's not too easy. Apartments are worse than in CPH and more expensive as well. I was succesful with booking an airbnb with some other Danish exchange students for the first 2 weeks and then we went apartment hunting upon our arrival. Some have been succesful with booking in advance for the whole period as well, but be aware of scammers.
We found an apartment through
realestate.com
. If you're lookling more solo, FB pages like Fairy Flossers and Flatmates are pretty good and people are nice.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer:
It was stressful to not find a place and keep going out to see places that were barely fit to live in. But in the end, it was so worth it. On-campus living/dorms are very expensive, so you can find better on your own if you have the guts and time for it. 
Also, if you're willing to share a room, you can cut a lot off the price. I had a roomie I knew from back home and because we were both busy exploring and traveling during the semester as well, we still had plenty of alone time.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Very expensive compared to what you get. Though, it gives a more safe arrival to know there's a place for you to live, so depends on priorities. I only knew a few exchange students that went with student accomodation.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: You get a lot of info and guides about how to apply and enroll after receiving your nomination. I had some issues with receiving my approval from UniMelb for my subjects, but it was all sorted out. I just had to be more proactive myself.

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: After receiving your nomination from UniMelb, they send you a guide about how to apply to study there. It's just a formality; as an exchange student with a nomination from KU, you get the spot you apply for. It takes some time to have it all settled, so don't stress and just follow deadlines. During the application process, you also apply for your student visa and overseas health care (OSHC), so everything becomes settled as you move along. After applying, you get a UniMelb user and can follow their online stepwise guide for completing your enrollment (applying for subjects etc.).

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: Stop1 (student help service at UniMelb)

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: Not really succesful at once. 3/4 of the subjects I wanted had requirements of prerequisite subjects, so I had to document that I was eligible for the subjects by documenting the previous subjects I'd had at KU. One of my required documents was missing, so instead of Stop1 reaching out to the subject coordinators on my behalf, I just had to e-mail them myself later. It was a bit stressful, since I only received notice of this in June, but everything was settled in July before the semester started.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Be ahead of deadlines, make sure you submit all the required documents, and enroll in the subjects you want as soon as possible. The subjects without prerequisites needed can be applied for as soon as you get your user, and if quotas apply, they fill up somewhat fast. The 1 subject I wanted with no prerequisites and quotas was full when I wanted to enrol, but I just wrote to the subject coordinator and asked if I could get a spot anyways, and then I was approved.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Have a look at the subjects catalogue for subjects outside your study. They have a lot of different, fun subjects (street art, wine subject, management subjects etc.)

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA classes while you were on exchange *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer:
There's 3 levels for BA: 1000 (1st year), 2000 (2nd year), 3000 (3rd year).
1st and 2nd year subjects have more attendance and a higher workload throughout the semester with small quizzes than what we're used to at KU. 3rd year subjects have more flexibility but not as much as we're used to at KU.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: All my lectures were streamed and saved online, so I could watch them on my own time as it suited me. Otherwise, there's a lot more control around the subjects than what I've been used to. Mid-semester tests are very common, as are assignments and quizzes during the semester. They all count towards your final grade, so when you have your end of semester exam, you already have some points towards passing, if you've done some work during the semester. Normally, I prefer doing everything on my own time as we pretty much do at KU, but at UniMelb, it gave more security to know the final exam didn't count 100%, since it made it easier to pass overall (all grades are transferred as passed/not passed to KU, so your grades at the host university do not count).

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
AGRI10039 Australia in the Wine World
PHRM20001 Pharmacology: How Drugs Work
NEUR30004 Complex Functions in Neuroscience
NEUR30005 Developmental Neurobiology

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
AGRI10039: very fun and different. Each week there's a prac class with is a wine tasting where attendance is required (I believe you have to be there for 8/10, but I recommend coming as much as possible since you learn a lot). Not just for fun; there's still curriculum and lectures, exam is divided into 1 theoretical and 1 prac, so you still have to learn the theoretics. Gives knowledge on wine in general and wine regions.

PHRM20001: intro subject to pharmacology. With a background in biomed, I knew a lot in advance, so it was a pretty easy subject to follow. It gives some new perspectives pharm-wise and in terms of therapies. The lecturers were very enthusiastic. A lot of repetition as well on general physiology. If you want a more academically challenging subject, I'd not recommend this. For me, it worked well with my other subjects since I had a big background knowledge so it gave me more time for exploring the city and traveling during the semester.

NEUR30004: not what I expected. The first half of lectures were not so well-organized and a bit confusing as to what they wanted us to actually learn. Almost philosophical about cognition, not science-oriented in my opinion (I did not enjoy this). Last half was very well-organized and interesting to me (about nociception and pain). If you're into neuroscience, it's an alright subject, last part at least was very fun. Mid-semester test was difficult, but end of semester test went smoothly so I wouldn't worry too much. Otherwise, I've heard great things of the 3rd year stem cell subject.

NEUR30005: by far my favorite subject. Well-organized, all lecturers were great, and it builds very well on Signal Transduction and other bio/pathway stuff learned with a background in biomed. 3 lectures every week, so you get a lot of knowledge, but no attendance required, so you can fit it in your schedule as you please. Lot of neuro stuff of course, but since they use research articles as the basis of the lectures, you also get are more plain biomed POV as well as cancer and what therapies/methods you in general can use.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: Visa and OSHC (5000 DKK in total) and plane tickets are expensive. So is living in AUS in general.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer:
Groceries are pricy, so is alcohol, but coffee is cheap and good. You can sign up to get free frozen meals (3-4 per week) and groceries from campus each week. It's not good food, but it's edible and you can save a lot on this.
Plane tickets are pretty cheap (if booked at least 2 weeks before departure), so it's easy to get around. Public transport is also cheap in Victoria if you're on your bachelor's; you can get a concession card and save 50% on all trams, busses and trains. I recommend this as it helps you get around easily, and Melbourne's a big city, if you want to go beyond inner city CBD (central business district). I think you pay a max. of 5$ a day with concession, otherwise I think it's 10$.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer:
I signed up for the gym at campus. Pretty cheap (less than 300DKK per month) loads of racks, machines etc., and always space if you steer clear of rush hour (5 PM ish). You also get access to their swimming pools, yoga/dance classes.
Otherwise, they also have loads of clubs. I didn't sign up for any because I was plenty busy without still. But they both have sports clubs and social clubs. Before the semester starts, the uni host intro-days where you can meet all the clubs and hear about what they do.
They have an exchange student society (MUSEX) as well that connects you with other exchange students.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: They have a mountaineering club which you can rent gear from if you join some of their trips in the beginning, pretty nice if you like hiking and have some experience. They also have a ski club where they go in trips, but you have to sign up pretty early for the good trips (already in April I think). Lastly, their surf club is very popular, too (especially for parties and stuff). All clubs have instagram, so go check them out in advance if you're curious, otherwise just show up for intro days

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer:
Take some time to get to know Melbourne. It's a wonderful city and I loved living there. Especially the neighborhoods around CBD (Fitzroy, Collingwood, Brunswick, Carlton, South Melbourne/Yarra, St Kilda) are lovely. I lived in South Melbourne and loved it. Loads of cafés and thrift shopping in Fitzroy/Collingwood/Brunswick/Chapel Street.

Victoria (the state Melbourne is located in) is beautiful and there's plenty to do on smaller trips (day/weekend). I can recommend Great Ocean Road, the Grampians, Wilsons Promontory, Camel's Hump, Hanging Rocks, Thousand Steps and Phillip Island. 
Otherwise, you can catch a plane and go further. Tasmania is beautiful and nearby, but a weekend is a bit too short I'd say. It's also pretty easy to get to Uluru/Ayer's Rock, but book in good time since plane tickets get expensive and before it gets too hot (October was good). Sydney is also just 1,5 h away by plane, you can also take bus/train, but it's 8-12h.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Very easy. Melbourne is very European in style. People are friendlier though.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer:
The Australian students kept a lot to themselves. Few came to lectures/class in general and they're a bit younger, so I mainly socialized with other exchange/international students. Though, the few Aussies that come to class are friendly, so try and chat with them if you want (especially easy in wine class). Otherwise, the clubs are a good way to meet other students, both local and exchange.
A lot of Danes were in Melbourne as well. We had messenger/Facebook groups to arrange meetings and ask questions about enrollment which was very nice.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: Not really anything culturally. Only thing that was difficult was being far away from home and finding a place to live in the beginning, but I got adjusted quickly and just had a lot of fun and kept busy.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: The friendliness and the good coffee. Also, being outdoors is a big part of the culture; people go a lot to the many parks, outside dining and rooftops are popular, and people are very active and do a lot of sports (bouldering, tennis courts, running etc.). We also found a paddle court in Docklands which was a chill way to hang out.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
1) Take your time with application for it to be less stressful
2) Enjoy the city, Melbourne is awesome
3) Travel around if you have the money/time

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: I appreciated that my exchange wasn't too academically challenging so I had time for fun stuff and traveling as well. It can also be overwhelming to live so far away, so it was nice to not have a hard time with studies as well.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: The travels. Overall, with the subjects I had, UniMelb was not as academically challenging as KU, but this can maybe be modified with other subjects. I studied much less than I usually would and still passed everything, no issues there. Just don't fall too behind, otherwise the exam period will be too tight.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Finding a place to live. Afterwards, everything went smoothly.

questions.question: Any other comments?
questions.answer: Best decision I made, best half year of my life. It's an amazing opportunity to try and live somewhere else than Denmark/far away, which is very fun and rewarding to try. Also a great way to see Australia/New Zealand, since it's not otherwise easy to get there and travel.

questions.question: Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
